name: Laskar Pelangi (The Rainbow Troops)
blurb: Andrea Hirata's novel of ten poor children and their tiny village school on Belitung
title: Laskar Pelangi Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending
description: Andrea Hirata's Laskar Pelangi explained: Ikal, Lintang, Mahar and Bu Mus, a full plot summary, the ending of the novel and of the 2008 film, and themes.
h1: Laskar Pelangi (The Rainbow Troops): Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Laskar Pelangi is an Indonesian novel by Andrea Hirata, published in 2005 by Bentang Pustaka and translated into English as The Rainbow Troops. It is narrated by Ikal, who looks back on his childhood at SD Muhammadiyah, a poor Islamic school in the village of Gantong on the tin-mining island of Belitung. Ten children from poor families and two devoted teachers keep the school alive against the odds. The book is the first of a series, became one of the best-selling Indonesian novels, and was made into a hugely popular film in 2008.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: Ikal
The narrator, a pupil who loves writing poetry
Lintang
A fisherman's son with a gift for mathematics who cycles a long way to school
Mahar
An artistic pupil fascinated by music, dance and the occult
Bu Mus (Muslimah Hafsari)
The young teacher who names the class the Laskar Pelangi
Pak Harfan (Harfan Efendy Noor)
The patient, kind headmaster of SD Muhammadiyah
Harun
An older boy with an intellectual disability who is the tenth pupil to enrol
Sahara
The only girl in the group, strong-willed and devout
Kucai
The class leader throughout their school years
Flo
A rich girl who transfers from the tin company's school
A Ling
A Kiong's cousin, a Chinese-Indonesian girl and Ikal's first love

body: The rest of the ten are A Kiong, Mahar's loyal follower; Syahdan, who dreams of becoming an actor; Borek, who is obsessed with being strong; and Trapani, a gentle boy very attached to his mother.

Opening day. Belitung is rich in tin, but almost all of that wealth goes to the state company PN Timah and its staff, who live behind fences and send their children to a well-equipped company school. SD Muhammadiyah in Gantong is the opposite: a leaning wooden building with a leaking roof. The education office has ruled that it will be closed if it cannot enrol ten new pupils. On the first day only nine children turn up. Just as Pak Harfan is about to announce that the school will close, Harun arrives with his mother, and the school survives.

The class. Ikal, Lintang, Mahar, Sahara, A Kiong, Syahdan, Kucai, Borek, Trapani and Harun stay together from the first year of primary school to the end of junior high. After the children see a rainbow, Bu Mus calls them the Laskar Pelangi, the Rainbow Troops. She and Pak Harfan teach for almost no pay, holding the school together with patience and faith.

Lintang. Lintang lives on the coast and cycles about forty kilometres each way to school, sometimes held up by crocodiles on the road, yet he is never late without reason. He turns out to be brilliant, solving problems faster than anyone, teachers included.

Mahar and the carnival. Mahar's love of art and of the supernatural often gets him teased. When the school enters the Independence Day carnival on 17 August, Mahar designs a costume dance inspired by the people of Papua, and the poor school wins the prize that the rich schools usually take.

First love. Ikal falls in love with A Ling after glimpsing her hand at the shop where he buys chalk. They exchange notes and poems until she leaves for Jakarta to care for her aunt, and he is heartbroken.
Flo. A rich, tomboyish girl named Flo leaves the PN Timah school to join SD Muhammadiyah and becomes part of the group.

The quiz. The school enters a regional academic quiz against the best schools on the island. Lintang answers question after question and, in the final, challenges a teacher from the PN Timah school, Drs. Zulfikar, over a disputed answer, and wins the argument. SD Muhammadiyah takes first place.

Not long after the quiz, Lintang's father, a poor fisherman, dies. Lintang is the eldest son, and he leaves school to work and feed his mother and younger siblings. He writes a farewell letter to his friends, and the class loses its brightest pupil just as his future seemed open.

The novel then jumps about twelve years ahead. Ikal has left Belitung and is scraping a living in Bogor, sorting mail at the post office before dawn. Returning home, he finds what became of the others: Lintang drives a truck; Kucai has become a member of the local parliament; Mahar, after years without work, is asked to record traditional children's games and goes on to write a novel; Syahdan works in computer networks; Trapani is in a psychiatric hospital. The book ends without wrapping up Ikal's own story, which continues in the sequels.

The 2008 film, directed by Riri Riza, ends differently. In 1999 the grown Ikal visits Belitung and meets Lintang, now married with a young daughter, and tells him he has won a scholarship to study at the Sorbonne in Paris. The film closes with the constitutional right of every citizen to an education.

Hirata has said the book is based on his own childhood and was written as a tribute to his teacher. Most readers take the ending as a double message: education changes lives, as it does for Ikal, but poverty can take that chance away from even the most gifted child, as it does for Lintang.

ul: Education as hope: a school with nothing but devoted teachers gives poor children the confidence to compete with the island's richest school.
Poverty and inequality: the tin wealth of Belitung stays inside the PN Timah fences while the villagers around it stay poor.
Teachers: Bu Mus and Pak Harfan work for almost nothing, and the book presents their dedication as the real reason the school survives.
Friendship: ten very different children, including Harun and the eccentric Mahar, become a group that sticks together through good and bad times.
Lost potential: Lintang's departure shows how family duty and poverty can end a brilliant child's education.
Length: the novel runs to over 500 pages in the Indonesian edition but is told in short, episodic chapters; the 2008 film runs about two hours (124 minutes).
Series: it is followed by Sang Pemimpi (2006), Edensor (2007) and Maryamah Karpov (2008); Sang Pemimpi and Edensor were also filmed.
Language and adaptations: written in Indonesian with Belitung Malay words; the film by Riri Riza, produced by Mira Lesmana, was followed by a stage musical and a television series.
Content: suitable for younger readers; the sad moments are a father's death and a child forced to leave school.

What teachers usually ask about: the novel's intrinsic elements (theme, setting, characters, point of view), the values it teaches about education and perseverance, the role of Bu Mus, and Lintang's fate.

check.q: Why was SD Muhammadiyah in danger of closing on the first day?
options: It needed ten new pupils and only nine had come
The tin company wanted the land
check.why: The school would be shut without ten new pupils, and Harun's late arrival made the tenth.

check.q: Which pupil designs the dance that wins the 17 August carnival?
check.why: Mahar, the class artist, creates the costume dance that beats the rich schools.

options: His father dies and he must support his family
He is expelled after the quiz
check.why: When his fisherman father dies, Lintang, the eldest son, has to work to feed the family.

faq.q: Is Laskar Pelangi a true story?
faq.a: It is a novel based closely on Andrea Hirata's own childhood in Gantong, Belitung, and on his teacher Muslimah; some events and characters are fictionalised.

faq.q: What happens to Lintang in Laskar Pelangi?
faq.a: After his father's death he leaves school to support his family; in the novel he later works as a truck driver, and in the film he is shown married with a daughter.

faq.q: What is the sequel to Laskar Pelangi?
faq.a: Sang Pemimpi (2006), which follows Ikal in senior high school, then Edensor (2007) and Maryamah Karpov (2008).
